title: Heat stroke: signs and what to do
asks: heat stroke what do i do
he collapsed in the heat and is confused

answer: Suspect heat stroke when someone in the heat or working hard becomes confused, acts strangely or aggressively, has convulsions or a seizure, or passes out. Poor or worsening mental status is a true medical emergency.

Other signs: repeated vomiting, loss of bowel control, limp or rigid muscles, weak or rapid pulse, rectal temperature above 104 °F. Ear, forehead, armpit and mouth temperature readings are not reliable.
Do not go by the skin: it may be hot and dry, or moist with sweat. Go by the mental state.
Call for emergency help and evacuation immediately (dial 911 or the local emergency number). Start cooling while you wait.
Lay the person down in the shade or the coolest place available, and raise the feet.
Remove as much clothing as possible.

Cool the person rapidly with the best method you have: pour water over the body while fanning; repeatedly wrap in iced sheets; put ice bags or cold packs on the torso, neck and scalp; or douse or immerse the person in cold water. A nearby stream or pond can be used.
Do not delay cooling: delay is the single most important factor leading to death or lasting disability. Do not wait to take a temperature.

Drinks: sources differ. FEMA says do not give a person with heat stroke anything to drink. The Army heat bulletin allows sips of water only if the person is conscious, fully alert and able to swallow without risk of choking or vomiting.
If the person is unconscious or barely responsive, place them on one side and watch the airway closely in case of vomiting.

Keep up rapid cooling until the person's mental state is back to normal (and the rectal temperature, if you can measure it, is down to 102 °F). After that, cooling can continue without cold water if needed. Keep checking: the temperature can rise again.
During transport, iced sheets (re-wetted and replaced), bags of ice or ice packs can be used. Do not interrupt iced-sheet cooling until the person reaches medical care.
Keep watching breathing, pulse and level of consciousness. If breathing stops and you cannot find a pulse, begin CPR if you are trained.
warnings: Give nothing to drink to a person who is confused, drowsy, unconscious or vomiting.
Do not give aspirin, acetaminophen or NSAIDs: fever medicines are not effective for heat stroke and may be harmful.
Heat stroke is life-threatening. Anyone suspected of heat illness must have cooling started early, in the field.
Even if the person seems to recover and the temperature returns to normal, get them to medical care as soon as possible: organ damage can still develop.

quotes.text: Exertional heat stroke Life-threatening condition characterized by CNS dysfunction (for example, delirium, agitation, inappropriate aggressiveness, convulsions or coma) that occurs in the presence of severe hyperthermia.

Upon first recognition of a significant heat casualty (confusion, combativeness, loss or decreased level of consciousness, inappropriate behavior, and/or recurrent vomiting; see Table 5–1), EMS should be activated.

Significant Signs and Symptoms • Persistent mental status changes • Delirium • Inappropriate behavior or aggressiveness • Convulsions and/or seizures • Coma • High rectal temperature (> 104 ºF) • Recurrent vomiting • Loss of bowel control/fecal incontinence • Flaccid muscles or persistent rigidity • Weak or rapid pulse

Service members involved in strenuous hot weather activity who present with associated symptoms (for example, unsteady gait, sweaty, flushed skin, dizzy, headache, tachycardia, paresthesia, weakness, nausea, cramps) should be immediately evaluated for vital signs, mental status changes, and rectal temperature. Poor or worsening mental status represents a true medical emergency, and these Service members need rapid initiation of effective cooling measures, activation of EMS, and evacuation to an MTF.

Rectal temperature is the only appropriate method to assess body core temperature of a heat casualty (see paragraph 3–2). Do not rely on ear, forehead, armpit, or oral temperature measurements as these are inaccurate (see Table 3–1).

In the past, heat stroke victims were described as always having hot, red, dry skin. However it has been found that some heat stroke victims may just as often as not be moist from sweat. Therefore, upon initial evaluation, the skin cannot be the differentiating factor in deciding on the degree of the heat injury.

In exertional heat stroke, perspiration may still be present. In general, the person suffering from heat stroke appears very ill and demonstrates an altered mental state including confusion, delirium, or coma.

Immediately call medical evacuation or ambulance for emergency transport while doing the following: • Lay casualty down in shade, elevate feet until medical evacuation or ambulance arrives • Remove as much clothing as possible • Cool rapidly using best method possible: - Pour water over body while fanning - Repeatedly wrap in iced sheets - Apply contour conforming ice bags/frozen gel packs covering torso, neck, and scalp - Douse or immerse in iced/cold water • If conscious, provide sips of water • If persistent hyperthermia not improving, and emergency evacuation delayed, start IV hydration • Monitor airway and breathing

If someone is suspected of having heat stroke, it is crucial to seek emergency medical help immediately. While waiting for medical professionals to arrive, follow these first aid steps: • Move the person to a cooler location: Get them out of the heat and into a shaded or air-conditioned area as quickly as possible. • Call for emergency assistance: Dial 911 or the appropriate local emergency number to request immediate medical help to include MEDEVAC.

Cool the person rapidly: Reduce their body temperature as quickly as possible. You can immerse the person in a tub of cold water, use ice cooling sheets or apply cold water to their body using wet towels or sponges. Fan the person while misting them with cool water to enhance cooling. • Monitor their vital signs: Keep a close eye on the person's breathing, pulse, and level of consciousness. If they stop breathing and you can no longer find a pulse, begin CPR if you are trained to do so.

All Service members suspected of having exertional heat illness must have early initiation of cooling in the field. Delay in cooling is the single most important factor leading to death or residual serious disability in those who survive. Do not delay cooling for want of rectal temperature. The casualty should lie down in the shade with as much clothing removed as is practical. Body cooling should be initiated as quickly as possible. Thirsty and alert patients can be given oral fluids (initially 1 quart per 30 minutes).

Extremely high body temperature, skin that is hot and red, dizziness and confusion, and a rapid and strong pulse are all heat stroke symptoms and may be a medical emergency. Call 9-1-1 or get the victim to a hospital immediately. Do not give the person anything to drink. Cool the person by removing their clothing and moving to a cooler environment. Try a cool bath, sponging, ice packs, or wrap in cold, wet sheets. Use fans and air conditioners, if available. Watch for breathing problems until emergency medical personnel arrive.
Oral fluids work well for most dehydrated patients who are not obtunded and can take fluids without risk of aspiration or vomiting.

Patients demonstrating combativeness, delirium (disturbance in attention and cognition), obtundation (reduced level of consciousness), or coma with severe hyperthermia most likely have EHS rather than EHI.

Aggressive whole-body cooling must be initiated as soon as possible, using the most practical and effective means available. First, the patient needs to lie down in the coolest location immediately available. An obtunded or comatose patient should be placed on one side with the airway closely monitored to avoid aspiration of vomitus.

EHS patients may experience loss of bowel control and vomiting; because of this, water immersion baths of all types should be disinfected between cases if they become contaminated with body fluids or discarded if easily disposable. Nearby streams or ponds can also be used effectively for the same purpose.
Aggressive cooling measures should continue until mental status returns to normal and body core temperature is 102 °F.

Rapid cooling of hyperthermic patients should continue until the rectal temperature remains below 102 °F, after which cooling can proceed without cold water (such as a tepid shower) until the rectal temperature remains below 100 °F, if needed.
After discontinuation of cooling, rectal temperature should be monitored every 5 minutes to ensure that it does not increase.

During evacuation, cold-water immersion is often not a viable method for treatment. Iced sheets (continuously replaced and rewetted; see Table 5–2), bags of ice, or refrigerated ice packs for covering the body can be used during transport.
overcooling with iced sheets is very unlikely - do not disrupt cooling with iced sheets until reaching definitive care.

The use of antipyretics is not effective and may potentially be harmful to EHS victims. Aspirin, an NSAID, and acetaminophen, an analgesic and antipyretic, both lower body core temperature by normalizing the elevated hypothalamic set point that regulates the fever response caused by pyrogens; with exertional heat illness, the set point is normal, with body core temperature elevation reflecting a failure of normal cooling mechanisms. Furthermore, acetaminophen may induce additional liver damage, and administration of aspirin may aggravate bleeding tendencies.

Since NSAIDs and acetaminophen do not attenuate body core temperature during environmental heat exposure and the toxicity of these drugs on the gut and liver is exacerbated with heat, the use of these drugs prophylactically or for the treatment of EHS patients is not warranted.

If the patient survives the first 24 hours, it is likely he or she will recover but may still develop liver and heart failure, kidney damage, and abnormalities with the clotting mechanisms of the blood. Therefore, even if the core temperature drops to the normal range, transport the patient to medical assistance as soon as possible.

conflict: (1) Drinks: FEMA P-2064 (2020) says of heat stroke 'Do not give the person anything to drink'; TB MED 507 (2022) Table 5-1 says 'If conscious, provide sips of water' and elsewhere limits oral fluids to 'thirsty and alert' patients who are 'not obtunded and can take fluids without risk of aspiration or vomiting'. The card shows both and warns against drinks for anyone who is not alert; the owner must choose. (2) Skin: ATP 4-02.11 (2026), ATP 3-50.21 (2018), FM 7-22 (2020) and FEMA list hot, dry or red skin without sweating as a sign, and HHS Ship's Medicine Chest (2003) says 'The skin feels hot and very dry' but adds 'In exertional heat stroke, perspiration may still be present'; TB MED 507 Table 4-3 says sweating is 'Typically present' in exertional heat stroke; ATP 4-25.12 says the skin 'cannot be the differentiating factor'. The card follows ATP 4-25.12 and says not to go by the skin. (3) Temperature: TB MED 507 lists rectal temperature above 104 F as a sign but says not to rely on a specific value and that only rectal readings are valid; ATP 4-02.11 says 'typically above 104' F; HHS says the temperature 'exceeds 40.6 C or 105 F'; ATP 4-25.12 calls a core temperature over 106 F with rectal over 108 F 'the most significant sign'. The card uses the TB MED 507 figure. (4) How long to cool: TB MED 507's end point (mental status normal and 102 F, then cooling without cold water, re-check every 5 minutes) is written in its hospital section; its field text says only that iced-sheet cooling should not be interrupted until definitive care; HHS says the victim 'must be carefully cooled following onshore medical advice'; FEMA and ATP 4-02.11 give no end point. The card applies the TB MED 507 end point in the field; the owner should confirm. Minor: 'Nearby streams or ponds' comes from TB MED 507's paragraph on field-expedient immersion baths.
